before: A bool stores true or false. && means both conditions must be true; || means at least one must be true; ! reverses true and false.
&& does not evaluate its right side when the left side is false. || does not evaluate its right side when the left side is true. This is short-circuit evaluation.
In denominator != 0 && 10 / denominator > 1, != means not equal. Checking the denominator first prevents division by zero when it is zero.

Parentheses group conditions. Use them when combining operators so the intended question is clear. The using System; directive makes names from the System namespace available, so Console means System.Console here; it does not execute the output operation.
Expected behavior from this example: True. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Try denominators 0, 2, and 20. Predict whether the division executes and what Boolean is printed before each run. You may trace it on paper if no C# toolchain is installed; reading completion does not certify a run.

Optional local setup: with the .NET10 SDK already installed, open a terminal in a new practice folder and run dotnet new console --framework net10.0. Replace that project’s Program.cs with the complete lesson example, then run dotnet run in the same folder. These commands create local project files; do not run them inside an existing project you want to preserve. The app itself does not compile C#.
after: A bool stores true or false. && requires both sides to be true. || requires at least one side to be true. ! changes true to false and false to true.
&& skips its right side when the left side is false. || skips its right side when the left side is true. This is called short-circuit evaluation: the answer is already known.
The condition denominator != 0 checks that the number is not zero. Putting that check before && can prevent the division on the right from running with zero.
using System brings names from the System namespace into view. A namespace groups names. Here it lets us write Console instead of System.Console; it does not run a printing instruction.
The denominator is 2, so the left check passes. The right side then divides 10 by 2. The result is 5, which is greater than 1. Both checks are true.
Order matters. The guard must run before the operation it protects. Parentheses can group combined conditions when their order would otherwise be unclear.

To run the example locally, use a new practice folder with the .NET 10 SDK. Run dotnet new console --framework net10.0, replace Program.cs with the example, then run dotnet run. The browser lesson only checks your understanding.
